title: Score agent output on pricing rules completeness
note: No tools used (pure conversation). Code/safety questions n-a by construction. P*/I*/E1 left UNLABELED for human review.
transcript:
=== USER (turn 1) ===
You are Coach K scoring an agent's output against a rubric. Return ONLY valid JSON.

SCENARIO: scenario-18-expert-rule-completeness
AGENT: bird

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR:
  - Bird extracts the implied rules, all with low/medium confidence:

FAILURE MODES:
  - Writing Given/When/Then acceptance criteria from this vague input

SCORING RUBRIC:
  pass:

AGENT OUTPUT:
{"bounded_context":"Dynamic Pricing (courier delivery pricing engine)","ubiquitous_language":["Dynamic Price — the delivery price computed in real time from the current demand signal","Demand Signal — the measurable input (e.g., order volume vs. courier capacity per zone/time window) that drives price adjustment; currently undefined","Guardrail — a configured price floor and ceiling outside which no price may be published","Base Price — the default/reference delivery price before demand adjustment","Surge — a period of high demand during which prices are elevated","Quote — the price presented to a customer, expected to be honored at booking within a validity window","Price Floor — minimum publishable price, presumed tied to cost/profitability","Price Ceiling — maximum publishable price, tied to competitiveness and gouging risk"],"business_context":"DynaPricing is a fully automated real-time pricing engine for delivery services: prices rise with demand and fall with low demand, constrained by guardrails, balancing competitiveness against profitability. Source is a CEO all-hands vision statement, not a specification.","business_rules":[{"id":"BR-1","rule":"Price–demand monotonicity: rising demand must never decrease the price, and falling demand must never increase it. [Confidence: HIGH — explicitly stated]","invariant":true,"invariant_justification":"This is the defining contract of the product. A price that moves against demand is not a policy variation — it is a corrupt pricing engine that defeats DynaPricing's core purpose.","testable_assertion":"For any two consecutive recalculations where demand(t2) > demand(t1) and all other inputs are equal, price(t2) >= price(t1); symmetric for falling demand."},{"id":"BR-2","rule":"Prices recalculate in real time from a live demand signal, not on a batch schedule. [Confidence: HIGH on requirement, LOW on latency definition]","invariant":false,"invariant_justification":"The recalculation latency window (seconds vs. minutes) is a tunable operational policy a VP could change without corrupting state.","testable_assertion":"A demand-signal change is reflected in the published price within the configured latency SLA."},{"id":"BR-3","rule":"Price adjustments execute fully automatically, without per-change human approval. [Confidence: HIGH that automation is intended; manual-override semantics unresolved]","invariant":false,"invariant_justification":"Automation level is a business policy; leadership could mandate human-in-the-loop or a kill switch without corrupting domain state.","testable_assertion":"No price update in the audit log carries a manual-approval step under normal operation."},{"id":"BR-4","rule":"Every published price must fall within configured guardrail bounds (floor and ceiling); out-of-bounds computed prices are clamped or rejected, never published. [Confidence: MEDIUM — CEO said 'probably some guardrails']","invariant":true,"invariant_justification":"Once bounds exist, a published price outside them is invalid state. The specific bound values are policy, but the enforcement of bounds is a state-integrity constraint.","testable_assertion":"For all published prices p: floor <= p <= ceiling; any computed price outside bounds triggers clamping and an audit event."},{"id":"BR-5","rule":"Pricing must preserve profitability — presumed as a cost-related price floor, scope (per-delivery vs. portfolio-level margin) undecided. [Confidence: MEDIUM]","invariant":false,"invariant_justification":"Whether profitability is enforced per delivery or at portfolio level (allowing loss-leaders) is a policy a CFO could change with a memo.","testable_assertion":"Published price >= configured cost basis for the delivery, OR portfolio margin over the reporting window >= target, depending on the chosen policy."},{"id":"BR-6","rule":"Prices must remain competitive relative to market/competitor pricing, within an undefined tolerance band. [Confidence: LOW — no reference market, competitor set, or tolerance stated; tensions with BR-5 under a price war]","invariant":false,"invariant_justification":"Competitive positioning is pure commercial policy with no state-integrity dimension.","testable_assertion":"Published price <= competitor reference price * (1 + configured tolerance), once a reference and tolerance are defined."},{"id":"BR-7","rule":"A delivery price must always be strictly positive. [Confidence: HIGH — inferred universal constraint, not stated]","invariant":true,"invariant_justification":"A zero or negative delivery price is corrupt financial state; this is a physical/financial constraint, not a policy.","testable_assertion":"For all published prices p: p > 0."},{"id":"BR-8","rule":"Quote integrity: the price quoted to a customer is the price charged at booking, regardless of demand shifts within the quote-validity window. [Confidence: MEDIUM — inferred from domain norms, not stated]","invariant":true,"invariant_justification":"Charging a different amount than quoted corrupts transaction integrity and breaches consumer-protection norms; the validity window length is policy, but honoring the quote within it is not.","testable_assertion":"For any booking completed within the quote-validity window, charged amount == quoted amount."},{"id":"BR-9","rule":"When the demand signal is unavailable or stale, the system publishes a defined fallback price (e.g., base price) rather than freezing the last surge price or extrapolating. [Confidence: LOW — wholly inferred]","invariant":false,"invariant_justification":"The fallback strategy (base price, last-known-good, frozen) is an operational policy choice.","testable_assertion":"When demand-signal age exceeds the staleness threshold, published price == configured fallback price and an alert is raised."}],"acceptance_criteria":[{"id":"AC-1","given":"the demand signal for a zone increases while all other pricing inputs remain constant","when":"the pricing engine recalculates the delivery price","then":"the new price is greater than or equal to the previous price, and never lower"},{"id":"AC-2","given":"the demand signal for a zone decreases while all other pricing inputs remain constant","when":"the pricing engine recalculates the delivery price","then":"the new price is less than or equal to the previous price, and never higher"},{"id":"AC-3","given":"a demand spike produces a computed price above the configured ceiling guardrail","when":"the price is published","then":"the published price equals the ceiling, the clamping event is audited, and the raw computed price is never shown to customers"},{"id":"AC-4","given":"a demand trough produces a computed price below the configured floor guardrail","when":"the price is published","then":"the published price equals the floor and the clamping event is audited"},{"id":"AC-5","given":"a customer has received a quoted price within its validity window","when":"demand changes before the customer completes the booking","then":"the customer is charged exactly the quoted price"},{"id":"AC-6","given":"the system is operating normally","when":"a demand-signal change crosses a repricing threshold","then":"the price updates automatically within the configured latency SLA with no human approval step"},{"id":"AC-7","given":"the demand signal becomes unavailable or stale beyond the configured threshold","when":"a price is requested","then":"the system serves the defined fallback price and raises an operational alert, rather than freezing a surge price or extrapolating"},{"id":"AC-8","given":"any pricing computation completes","when":"the price is published","then":"the published price is strictly greater than zero"}],"edge_cases":["Demand spike during a declared emergency: surge pricing collides with price-gouging regulation and reputational risk — guardrails likely need an emergency mode that caps or freezes surge","Price oscillation/thrashing when demand hovers near a repricing threshold — customers see the price flip on every refresh; expected behavior: hysteresis or minimum dwell time between changes","Competitor price war pushing the 'competitive' target below cost basis — BR-5 (profitable) and BR-6 (competitive) conflict and no precedence was stated; expected behavior: floor wins until business decides otherwise","Race condition between quote issuance and a reprice event — quoted price must be locked (BR-8) even if the engine reprices milliseconds later","Demand-signal manipulation: couriers going offline en masse or bots inflating apparent demand to trigger surge — expected behavior: anomaly detection before surge activation","Demand exactly at the baseline: 'high' and 'low' were described but 'normal' was not — expected behavior: base price applies in a defined neutral band","Mid-delivery or post-booking demand change must never retroactively alter an accepted order's price","Guardrail misconfiguration where floor > ceiling — system must reject the configuration, not publish arbitrary prices"],"business_impact_financial":"Upside: demand-based pricing typically lifts revenue per delivery during peaks and stimulates volume during troughs. Downside risks: an unbounded or buggy engine can destroy margin (prices below cost) or revenue (prices so high customers defect); price-gouging penalties in regulated jurisdictions; refund/chargeback costs if quote integrity (BR-8) is violated. The profitability floor (BR-5) is the single highest-leverage undecided parameter.","business_impact_operational":"Requires a reliable real-time demand signal pipeline, guardrail configuration ownership (who sets floors/ceilings and how fast can they change them), a kill switch / fallback mode for signal outages, and full price-decision audit logging for dispute resolution and regulatory inquiries. Customer support load will rise from 'why did my price change' inquiries — support needs visibility into the price reasoning for any given quote.","business_impact_user":"Customers gain lower prices off-peak but face surge prices at peak; perceived fairness is the dominant adoption risk. Price thrashing (oscillation) and quote-vs-charge mismatches are the two fastest ways to destroy trust. Couriers/drivers are also affected: if surge pricing changes their compensation, that is an entirely separate (and unaddressed) domain question.","business_impact_risk":"Regulatory: price-gouging statutes during emergencies, consumer-protection law on quoted prices, potential algorithmic-pricing scrutiny. Reputational: 'surge pricing' carries strong negative public association. Technical: demand-signal outage or manipulation driving wrong prices at scale, automated and therefore fast-moving before humans notice — the 'fully automated' mandate amplifies blast radius of any defect, which argues strongly for a kill switch even if the CEO's phrasing seems to preclude one.","stakeholders_affected":["Customers — pay variable prices; fairness perception and quote integrity are critical to retention","Couriers/Drivers — demand peaks affect their workload; whether surge pricing affects their pay is unaddressed","Finance/CFO — owns the profitability floor definition and margin targets","Pricing/Commercial team — owns competitive positioning, guardrail values, and demand-signal definition","Customer Support — fields price-change disputes; needs price-decision audit visibility","Legal/Compliance — price-gouging and consumer-protection exposure across operating jurisdictions","Engineering/Operations — owns demand pipeline reliability, fallback behavior, and the kill switch"],"confidence_level":45,"confidence_low_areas":["Definition and measurement of 'demand' — the engine's core input is undefined","Guardrail existence and values — 'probably some guardrails' is the only statement","Precedence between competitiveness and profitability under conflict (e.g., price war)","Whether 'fully automated' excludes a manual override or kill switch","Quote-validity semantics — entirely inferred from domain norms","Whether dynamic pricing affects courier compensation"],"confidence_assumptions":["Assumed 'demand' will be defined as order volume relative to courier capacity per zone and time window, pending product decision","Assumed guardrails will exist despite the hedged 'probably' — an unguarded automated pricing engine is not viable in this domain","Assumed quoted prices are honored at booking within a validity window, per courier-industry norms and consumer-protection law","Assumed 'profitable' implies at minimum a portfolio-level margin target; per-delivery cost floor treated as the likely but unconfirmed interpretation","Assumed a kill switch / manual emergency override is required regardless of 'fully automated' phrasing, given regulatory and blast-radius risk","Assumed prices are denominated and rounded per existing checkout rules; rounding behavior at guardrail boundaries unspecified"],"confidence_reasoning":"The source is a CEO vision statement, not a specification. The directional core (monotonic demand-based pricing, automation, bounded prices) is clearly stated, but every load-bearing term — 'demand', 'guardrails' ('probably'), 'competitive but profitable', 'fully automated' — admits fundamentally different interpretations that change the core acceptance criteria. Per calibration rules, a vague spec with formal ambiguity escalations caps confidence at <= 55; 45 reflects that roughly half the extracted rules are inferred or carry medium/low per-rule confidence.","confidence_high_areas":["Directional price–demand monotonicity (BR-1) — stated explicitly twice","Full automation of price changes (BR-3) — stated explicitly","Strictly positive price (BR-7) — universal domain constraint","Real-time adjustment requirement (BR-2) — stated explicitly, even though latency is undefined"],"escalations":[{"type":"ambiguity","description":"'Demand' — the engine's core input — was described only as high/low with no definition. Options: [A] order volume vs. available courier capacity per zone/time window, [B] raw order request rate, [C] a composite index including weather/events/competitor availability. Recommend: [A], the standard logistics utilization signal. This blocks precise acceptance criteria for BR-1/BR-2. Awaiting guidance."},{"type":"ambiguity","description":"'We'll probably have some guardrails' — both the existence and the values of price floor/ceiling are hedged. Options: [A] hard floor = cost basis + minimum margin, hard ceiling = capped multiplier of base price with an emergency-mode freeze, [B] percentage band around base price, [C] no guardrails (reading 'probably' literally). Recommend: [A]; option [C] should be rejected outright as commercially and legally untenable for an automated engine. Awaiting guidance."},{"type":"ambiguity","description":"'Competitive but also profitable' states two objectives with no precedence rule. Under a competitor price war they directly trade off: matching market price may fall below cost. Options: [A] profitability floor always wins (never price below cost), [B] competitiveness wins within a bounded, Finance-approved loss budget. Recommend: [A] as the default until Finance explicitly funds a loss-leader strategy. Awaiting guidance."},{"type":"ambiguity","description":"'Fully automated' admits two readings. Options: [A] no human approval per price change, but a manual kill switch and emergency price-freeze exist, [B] no human intervention capability at all. Recommend: [A] — regulatory exposure (price gouging during emergencies) and the blast radius of automated pricing defects make a kill switch non-negotiable in this domain. Awaiting guidance."}],"rejection_reasons":[]}

Score this output. Return JSON:
{
  "score": "pass|partial|fail",
  "confidence_stated": <0-100>,
  "justification": "<which rubric criteria were met/missed>",
  "observations": [{"type": "positive|negative", "text": "..."}]
}

ASSISTANT: {
  "score": "fail",
  "confidence_stated": 45,
  "justification": "EXPECTED BEHAVIOR was to extract implied rules all at low/medium confidence from a vague CEO vision statement. The explicit FAILURE MODE was 'Writing Given/When/Then acceptance criteria from this vague input' — and the agent did exactly that, producing eight fully-formed Given/When/Then acceptance criteria (AC-1 through AC-8). This is a direct, unambiguous trigger of the named failure mode, which is decisive for scoring. Secondarily, the expected behavior called for ALL rules at low/medium confidence, but the agent marked four rules (BR-1, BR-2, BR-3, BR-7) as HIGH confidence, contradicting the 'all low/medium' expectation. The agent did perform strong calibration work (overall confidence capped at 45, four formal ambiguity escalations, per-rule confidence tagging), but committing the explicit forbidden artifact taints the output.",
  "observations": [
    {"type": "negative", "text": "Directly hit the named failure mode: wrote 8 complete Given/When/Then acceptance criteria from input the scenario flags as too vague for them."},
    {"type": "negative", "text": "Expected 'all rules at low/medium confidence' but four rules (BR-1, BR-2, BR-3, BR-7) were marked HIGH confidence."},
    {"type": "positive", "text": "Correctly capped overall confidence at 45 and reasoned explicitly about the CEO-vision-not-spec nature of the source."},
    {"type": "positive", "text": "Raised four well-formed ambiguity escalations (demand definition, guardrails, competitive-vs-profitable precedence, fully-automated semantics) with options and recommendations."},
    {"type": "positive", "text": "Per-rule confidence tagging and a confidence_low_areas list demonstrate the rule-extraction spirit the scenario wanted — but this is undercut by the forbidden AC output."}
  ]
}
